BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, the game trailer, 32 terms for making a short film that sells a game you built from the hook to the call to action, knowing the exact term lets you tell an editor or an AI coding agent precisely what to change.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often think a trailer shows the game they plan to make. It does not. A trailer shows real play from the build you have, builds to one peak, and ends on one action. A plan feature on screen is a promise you cannot keep. This film goes through the terms of making a trailer, each one shown.

BDEFS.heard: Eight labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Outside source, the term comes from a source outside the course text, computed. The numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured, conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 32 terms for a short film that sells a game in four groups. The first group is what you are making. Trailer, teaser, gameplay video, pitch film, pitch, log line, tag line, hook, key art and thumbnail. The kind of film and the idea it sells.

B0102.heard: The second group is shape and length, beat structure, climax, title card, call to action, logo sting, runtime, frame rate and resolution. These terms say where each part of the film goes and how long it runs.

B0103.heard: The third group is cutting and sound, pacing, cut on action, BPM, which means beats per minute, cut on the beat, music drop, sound design and muted test. These terms say how the cuts and the music work together.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Capture and Honesty, fixed frame rate, movie maker mode, clean footage, gameplay versus cinematic, honest trailer, viewer test and accessibility. These terms cover getting real footage of your game and keeping the promise the film makes.

B0201.heard: A chart of film lengths from 0 to 600 seconds. A trailer is a short film that sells a game to a stranger, someone who owes you nothing. It shows the best real moments and ends on one action. Store trailers run 30 to 90 seconds at the top bar. For example, you cut together the best moments of your platformer, the jump, the spikes, the goal flag and end on one line that says where to play it.

B0202.heard: A teaser is an early look that hints at a game and shows little. It announces the game and saves the rest for later. Its bar is the short one 15-45 seconds and that range is made up for this example. A trailer sells and a teaser only hints. For example, before your game has a finished level, you post a short clip of the hero's silhouette in one jump, then the title, and nothing more.

B0203.heard: A gameplay video is playing footage of play made to cover the game not to sell it. It shows play as it is and makes no argument. Its bar is the long one three to ten minutes, a range that is also made up. For example, you record yourself playing the first level of your game from start to finish, with no cuts and no music, so a reviewer can see exactly how it plays.

B0204.heard: A pitch film argues for a project. It tells a reviewer what you will build and why, and in this course it runs two to four minutes the red bar. It is about a project not a finished game for sale. For example, you show captured play of the one room your game has today, then say what the final project will add, labeling what exists and what will exist.

B0301.heard: A block of text with a red bar for its length for a made-up game called Tilt. A pitch is a short sales description of the game idea, a few sentences long. This one is 32 words, it says what the game is, what is new, and how long a level takes. For example, the few sentences at the top of your game design document, telling a classmate while your platformer is worth playing are its pitch.

B0302.heard: A second shorter block and bar, a log line is the game in one sentence who does what and what is new. Hear the pitches cut from 32 words to 13, a platformer where you reverse gravity to turn every hazard into a pathway. For example, if your game is a platformer where the player swaps places with their own shadow to cross gaps, that one sentence, the kind you would say to a recruiter, is its log line.

B0303.heard: A tagline is a few memorable words that sit beside the title. Fall up is only two words. It cannot explain the game, it can only be remembered. A logline explains and a tagline does not. For example, under the title on your game's poster you might print the words one more jump. Nobody could work out how the game plays from them, and that is fine for a tagline.

B0401.heard: A drawing that builds one sentence from a mechanic. The hook is the most distinctive thing the player does said in one sentence. It names what you do and what that changes. Here you reverse gravity to turn hazards into pathways, eight words. A tagline is memorable words and a hook is the one thing nobody else has. For example, if the player in your game can freeze an enemy and stand on it, the hook is freeze an enemy to make your next step.

B0402.heard: Two openings on a timeline with a red line at five seconds. The hook test asks for gameplay in the first five seconds. In this made up example, the first opening is spends that time on black in a studio logo, so play starts at six seconds and it fails. Opening B starts on play and passes. For example, open the trailer for your platformer on the player already in the air over the spikes, not on your team's name.

B0403.heard: A poster key art is the one still image that stands for the game with a title, one character, and one idea. Here the title tilt, a single block for the character, a red triangle pointing the other way for gravity flipped in the tagline at the bottom. For example, for your platformer you might draw the hero leaping over a pit of spikes with the title above as the one image on the game's store page.

B0404.heard: The same poster at three sizes. A thumbnail is the small preview image, the key art at store size, and it has to read a glance. The title shrinks with the image. At 300 pixels wide it reads. At 45 pixels wide it is too small by a made up threshold of 12 pixels. For example, shrink your game's poster to the size of a store tile, and check that the title can still be made out.

B0501.heard: A timeline of the shipping lane trailer 30.5 seconds long. Beat structure is the order of a trailer's parts. Hook establish Escalate Peak title button call to action. Each part has a length and the lengths add up to the runtime. For example, in a trailer for your platformer, the hook is one striking jump. Establish shows the controls, Escalate adds enemies, and the peak is the last run to the goal.

B0502.heard: Now the peak is lit in red. The climax or peak is the biggest payoff placed on a strong beat of the music after a quiet drop. Here the music drops from 19 to 20 seconds and the peak starts at 20 seconds. That is beat 40, exactly 10 bars of 4, a downbeat. For example, in your trailer, the moment the player clears the last spike and lands beside the goal flag can be the climax.

B0503.heard: A title card is a held card with the game's name and it comes after the peak, not at the start. Here it holds for 1.5 seconds 45 frames at 30 frames per second. The name of a game nobody knows is the least interesting way to open. For example, right after your player lands the final jump, cut to your game's name in large letters on a playing card.

B0601.heard: Bars on an axis from 0 to 120 seconds. Runtime is how long the film runs. A store trailer is typically 30 to 90 seconds, and 60 to 90 is a good first target. The trailer gate and automatic check accepts 15 to 120. Shipping lane runs 30.5. For example, if your trailer shows the same jump in three shots, cutting two of them shortens the runtime without losing anything.

B0602.heard: Two rows of ticks, one second of film each. Frame rate is how many frames are shown each second. Frames are frame rate times seconds, so the 30.5 second film is 915 frames at 30 and 1830 at 60. For example, if your game is captured at 60 frames per second, every second of the players run as stored as twice as many pictures as at 30.

B0603.heard: A small gray frame inside a large pink one. Resolution is the width and height of each frame in pixels. 4K has four times the pixels of 1080p so it needs a stronger machine to capture. Frame rate is images per second and resolution is pixels per image. For example, the trailer gate wants native 4K footage so you run your game at that full size while you capture it, not in a small window.

B0701.heard: Nine shots before the title with lengths from the shipping lane shot list. Pacing is how fast the cuts come, counted in cuts per minute. It rises toward the peak but only after the viewer understands the game. Here it goes from 20 to 25.7 to 30. For example, you hold the first shots of your platformer long enough to show the controls, then cut faster as the enemies pile up before the final jump.

B0702.heard: A jump arc simulated with made-up inputs. Cut on action means cutting while a motion is underway so the eye carries across the cut. Before the jump out of the speed is zero. At the top, be it is 24 pixels a frame. Two frames after take off at C, it is 41, cut at C. For example, cut just after your player leaves the ground and open the next shot with the player still rising.

B0801.heard: Three rows of beat ticks over four seconds. BPM beats per minute is the tempo of the music. 60 divided by it gives the seconds between beats. At 90 BPM a beat comes every 0.667 seconds. At 120 every half second. At 140 every 0.429. For example, you check the music you picked for your trailer, find it as 120 BPM. And no a beat falls every half second.

B0802.heard: Rough cuts on top, a beat grid at 120 BPM and snapped cuts below. Cut on the beat means placing each cut on a beat of the music, so picture and sound locked together. In this made up example, five of nine cuts started near a beat, and after snapping all nine R. For example, the cut from your title screen to the first jump moves a few frames later, so it lands exactly on a drum hit.

B0803.heard: Bars for the loudness of the shipping lane music from its own measurements. The music drop is a quiet moment just before the peak, so the peak lands. The build is 0.14, the drop 0.016, about 18.8 decibels quieter, then the peak at 0.17. For example, the music in your trailer falls almost silent while your player hangs over the final gap, then returns as they land.

B0901.heard: A line for the music's loudness over three seconds. Sound design is how you mix, so the music sets the tone and the game's own hits punch through. At each hit the music steps down six decibels then recovers. That depth is made up for this example. For example, when your player stomps an enemy, the stomp sound comes through clearly while the music dips under it for a moment.

B0902.heard: Seven voice lines from the shipping lane shot list each with a tick. The muted test checks that the film still makes sense with the sound off. Every voice line is also shown on screen, so zero of seven are lost. Sound design is about the mix, and the muted test is about no sound at all. For example, you watch your trailer on mute, and if the voice says press space to jump, the screen shows it too.

B0903.heard: Two strips of bright frames and a caption box. Accessibility means more people can watch the film with captions for speech and no rapid flashing. A common limit is no more than three flashes in any second. In this made up example, the first sequence A has four in its worst second, too many in sequence B has two. For example, if your trailer flashes the screen white on every explosion, count the flashes before you cut and caption every spoken line.

B1001.heard: The end card of the shipping lane trailer, it's last 5.5 seconds. The call to action is one thing to do next, wishlist play or follow a link. Here it is one button, download on GitHub, held for 165 frames, 18% of the runtime. One action, not for social handles and no fade to black. For example, end your trailer on your game's title in one line, play it in the browser, held long enough to read.

B1002.heard: Two openings over the first 10 seconds. A logo sting is a very short logo animation with a sound, and it belongs at the end. But first, it leaves seven seconds of play instead of 10, so in this made-up example, the viewer sees 30% less play before deciding. A call to action asks for something, and a sting only signs the work. For example, play your team's short animated logo with its chime after the end card, never before the first jump.

B1101.heard: Two rows of frames, three seconds of play on a slow machine. A fixed frame rate locks rendering to a set number of frames a second, so every frame is the same slice of game time and runs match. Each frame here takes a made up 50 milliseconds to draw. In real time, 60 frames reach the file, fixed at 60, all 180 do, for example. A command line test of your game at a fixed 60 frames a second gives the same result on any laptop.

B1102.heard: A command typed in a terminal. Movie Maker Mode is Godose Mode that records a run to video file frame by frame at the rate you fix. The right movie flag names the file. The fixed frames per second flag set 60 and quit after stops at 1,800 frames 30 seconds of play. For example, to capture your platformer's first level for a trailer, you run it with these flags and get a smooth video file even on a slow laptop.

B1103.heard: One captured frame from a game, clean footage is real play with the debug clutter hidden, and any HUD the heads up display kept where it explains a mechanic. Here the frames per second counter, the collider overlay and a debug printer hidden three of five items while the token counter and the retry stay. For example, before you record your game, turn off the collision shapes you showed for testing, but keep the coin counter.

B1201.heard: A list of what trailer footage may be. Gameplay vs. Cinematic is the rule that footage is captured play from the real build, and a cinematic is allowed only if it is the game's own and is labeled. A rehearsed input route and the best of several takes are allowed. Teleporting invincibility and mock-up footage are not. For example, the cut-senior game really plays at the end of a level may appear labeled, but a fly-through rendered outside the game may not.

B1202.heard: A feature list made up for this example. An honest trailer shows only what the game really does and plan features never appear. Your jump, bump, block, shield, and stomp are implemented and may appear. Checkpoints are only planned so they never do 4 or 5. A trailer is a promise and the game has to keep it. For example, if your double jump works only in a test scene and not in the build, leave it out.

B1203.heard: A plan for two viewers with results still pending. The viewer test means showing the cut unexplained to someone new, stopping at 10 seconds and asking what kind of game it is and what the player does. One viewer watches with sound, one without. You already know the game so you cannot judge the cut yourself. Nobody has run this test yet. For example, show your trailer to a classmate who has never played your game and where their attention drifts cut.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets look alike terms side by side. A trailer sells the game and shows enough to convince. Here are 12 shots in 60 seconds, ending on one action. A teaser announces it and saves the rest. Three shots in 20 seconds, ending on a hint.

B1302.heard: A log line is one sentence that explains the game hear thirteen words. A tag line is a few words to remember and it explains nothing. Fall up is two words. Ask whether a stranger could tell how the game plays from it.

B1303.heard: Cut on action cuts while the motion is moving. At point C the jump moves 41 pixels a frame and at point A0. Cut on the beat cuts when the music pulses. A rough cut at 5.87 seconds snaps to 6.

B1304.heard: Key Art is the full still image that stands for the game with a title 64 pixels tall. A thumbnail is the same art at store size, where that title shrinks to about 26 pixels. Same picture smaller and it still has to read.

B1401.heard: Vague requests on the left exact instructions under them and what each one does on the right. Make the trailer shorter becomes cut it from 90 seconds to 60, 1,800 frames at 30 frames per second. That is 900 fewer frames, a third less.

B1402.heard: Make it more exciting becomes shortened shots from 3 seconds to 1.5 toward the peak after the game is shown. That doubles the pace from 20 to 40 cuts a minute. The floor for a shot is 0.8 seconds.

B1403.heard: Put it on the music becomes at 120 BPM, move every cut to the nearest half second beat. Cuts that were up to 170 milliseconds off the beat end at zero, with nine cuts on the grid.

B1404.heard: Start strong becomes show gameplay by 5 seconds and put the logo last. With the logo first, play starts at 6 seconds, which misses the limit by 1 second. With gameplay first, play starts at 0.

B1405.heard: Tell them what to do becomes end-on-one action held 5.5 seconds with the title, the platform and one link. In a 30.5 second film that is 18% of the runtime, 165 frames, long enough to read, short enough to keep.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before a trailer goes out. First, does real gameplay show in the first five seconds? If a logo or a fade comes first, move it to the end.

B1502.heard: Second, can you say the hook in one sentence, what the player does and what that changes. If you cannot, the trailer cannot find it either, and the problem is in the design.

B1503.heard: Third is every shot readable and are the cuts on the beat. Hold each shot long enough to follow, then snap each cut to the beat grid of the music.

B1504.heard: Fourth is every shot real play from this build. A rehearsed route and the best of several takes are fine. Mockups, invincibility and plan features are not.

B1505.heard: Fifth, does it work with the sound off with no rapid flashing? Run the muted test, then count the flashes in every second of the film.

B1506.heard: Sixth, is there one call to action held long enough to read? Then say it exactly. Not make it exciting, but one and a half second shots into the peak.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, a trailer sells a game to a stranger and a teaser only hints. A log line explains the game in one sentence and a tagline is only remembered. Show real gameplay in the first five seconds and put the logo last. The peak lands on a strong beat right after a quiet music drop. Cut on action follows the motion and cut on the beat follows the music. An honest trailer shows only real play from the build never planned features.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on trailer terms with short cases about making a trailer for a game I built one at a time. Use the terms trailer, teaser, logline, tagline, hook, climax, title, card, call to action, cut on action and cut on the beat. For each case I must name the exact term and say why it's look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply.

BOUT.heard: Key terms the game trailer at Nick Bear Brown.
